title: When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting

paper.title:
When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of
pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
paper.abstract:
Abstract Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed
recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes
at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense,
sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles.
This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far
fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves.
PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing : it
redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it
together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing
loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only
optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this
capture structure , not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes,
hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits
inherent to the formulation: SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom,
so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops
short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it.
A viable design must add back Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors,
retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Gaussian splatting [ 13 ] has made high-quality novel-view synthesis of real scenes routine, and with it the need for accurate camera poses at scale. The default recipe passes images through a structure-from-motion (SfM) system, almost always COLMAP [ 21 ] , before training. For large exterior scenes this SfM step is the bottleneck: robust incremental reconstruction of thousands of drone frames can take hours. The captures used for exterior splatting are, however, far from the “images-in-the-wild” regime SfM is built for: as above, a home is flown as several dense overlapping orbits, every frame carries GPS, and consecutive frames overlap strongly. It is natural to ask whether this structure lets us avoid the expensive part of SfM. Bundle adjustment [ 23 ] jointly refines camera poses and a large point cloud, its cost nominally dominated by the points: each 3D point adds three parameters and there are far more points than cameras. If we could constrain the cameras directly , through a dense graph of pairwise relative-pose measurements, the optimization would touch only the six degrees of freedom per camera and be both smaller and trivially decomposable per sequence. This intuition can be sharpened, and it is what makes a pose-only formulation tempting rather than naive. Each Gauss–Newton step of bundle adjustment [ 9 ] solves a normal-equation system that, with the camera update Δ ​ 𝐱 c \Delta\mathbf{x}_{c} ordered above the landmark update Δ ​ 𝐱 p \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p} , takes the block form [ B E E ⊤ C ] ​ [ Δ ​ 𝐱 c Δ ​ 𝐱 p ] = [ 𝐯 𝐰 ] , \begin{bmatrix}B&E\\ E^{\top}&C\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}\\ \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{v}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}, (1) with a camera block B B , a landmark block C C , and their coupling E E . Because C C carries one 3 × 3 3\times 3 diagonal block per 3D point it is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, so BA does not in fact pay for the landmarks directly: it eliminates Δ ​ 𝐱 p \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p} by the Schur complement, left-multiplying Eq. 1 by [ I − E ​ C − 1 0 I ] \left[\begin{smallmatrix}I&-EC^{-1}\\ 0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right] to reach the much smaller, pose-only reduced system ( B − E ​ C − 1 ​ E ⊤ ) ⏟ S ​ Δ ​ 𝐱 c = 𝐯 − E ​ C − 1 ​ 𝐰 , \underbrace{\big(B-EC^{-1}E^{\top}\big)}_{\textstyle S}\,\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}=\mathbf{v}-EC^{-1}\mathbf{w}, (2) and only then back-substitutes Δ ​ 𝐱 p = C − 1 ​ ( 𝐰 − E ⊤ ​ Δ ​ 𝐱 c ) \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p}=C^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-E^{\top}\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}) . Forming the reduction and back-substituting are redone at every iteration, so the dominant work is the repeated solve of S S , not the landmarks. If BA’s expensive core is already a pose-only system, the attractive idea is to build S S directly , as a pose graph of relative-pose constraints, skipping the landmark bookkeeping and marginalization altogether and arriving at the reduced system for free ( Fig. 1 ). The core question is whether the S S that pose-graph optimization assembles directly approaches the S S that BA produces by marginalization, in the limit of increasingly many inter-frame constraints. Figure 1 : The pose-only intuition. Bundle adjustment (left) couples the camera poses to a large landmark cloud through observation edges. Because the landmark block C C is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, BA marginalizes the landmarks via the Schur complement into a much smaller, pose-only reduced system S = B − E ​ C − 1 ​ E ⊤ S=B-EC^{-1}E^{\top} (right), solves it for the poses, and only then back-substitutes for the points. Since BA’s expensive core is already this pose-only system, a pose-only formulation tries to assemble S S directly from inter-pose relative-pose constraints (dashed), skipping the landmark detour. Both routes target the same S S ; this paper asks whether the shortcut recovers bundle-adjustment-grade poses. There is a further, more principled reason to study this here. Pose-graph optimization is a mature and well-understood tool [ 11 ] , but in robotics and SLAM [ 4 ] it is almost always a back-end refinement : a front end (visual odometry or SLAM) first produces poses of reasonable accuracy, and PGO then uses loop-closure edges to redistribute the accumulated drift into a globally consistent trajectory. Its power grows with the number and diversity of those loop closures. Splatting captures sit at an extreme of that regime: because the imagery is so dense, essentially every frame closes loops with dozens of others, so the pose graph is far richer than the sparse loop-closure graphs PGO is usually handed. This invites a genuine research question, in the limit of an ever-denser loop-closure graph, does pose-only optimization converge to bundle-adjustment accuracy? If it did, the dense structure of splatting captures would be exactly the setting in which to trade BA for PGO. We treat answering this, empirically and then structurally, as the study’s core purpose. This is the hypothesis we set out to validate: that dense pose-graph optimization, used not as a post-hoc SLAM refinement but as the primary estimation objective, can recover poses of BA-grade quality on these structured, GPS-tagged drone captures , faster and in a cloud-parallel form . We built the system and ran it on self-captured drone scenes and a public benchmark. The strong form of the hypothesis proved false. This paper explains why, using the system’s own design and numbers, and is careful about which parts of the explanation generalize: two of the causes are properties of the pose-only formulation that no parameter setting escapes, while the rest are choices this pipeline made and a better one could revisit. We keep the two apart throughout ( Sec. 5 ). We recall the related landscape ( Sec. 2 ), the pipeline ( Sec. 3 ) and its outcomes ( Sec. 4 ), then give the methodological failure analysis that is our contribution ( Sec. 5 ) and the design lessons it implies ( Sec. 6 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: COLMAP [ 21 ] is the de facto general-purpose standard for pose estimation in vision and the default front end for splatting. We do not aim to replace it there: we target only the narrow, structured regime of exterior splatting captures, using COLMAP as the reference a specialized pose-only design must match. GLOMAP [ 19 ] showed that global SfM can approach incremental accuracy at lower cost, yet COLMAP remains the method of choice when robust registration is required. Theia [ 22 ] offers both incremental and global SfM but is chiefly a researcher’s toolkit. Learned, feed-forward estimators such as VGGT [ 24 ] and Depth-Anything-3 [ 16 ] predict poses, depth and intrinsics in a single pass and are advancing quickly. They make excellent one-shot pose initializers, but as we confirm below they have not yet reached the pose accuracy of a robust system that nonlinearly refines poses. Our matching front end follows hierarchical localization [ 20 ] , pairing SuperPoint features [ 6 ] with LightGlue [ 17 ] and NetVLAD [ 2 ] retrieval indexed with FAISS [ 7 ] , a modern replacement for bag-of-words retrieval [ 8 ] . Distributing SfM across machines dates back to Building Rome in a Day [ 1 ] . Our design differs in demoting bundle adjustment [ 23 ] from the global objective to a per-chunk step and making pose-graph optimization carry the estimation, solved with g2o [ 14 ] (GTSAM [ 5 ] is the common alternative), and in exploiting GPS and sequential capture. It is the limits of that partial substitution, and of the pure-pose formulation it approximates, that we analyze.

sections.heading: 3 The system we built
sections.text: We summarize the pipeline only enough to make the analysis precise. It is not a general-purpose SfM system but one built expressly around the structure of these captures, dense sequential overlap, per-frame GPS, and multi-orbit coverage; a three-stage divide–compute–merge design ( Fig. 2 ). Figure 2 : System overview. The image stream is split into per-sequence chunks that are optimized independently as dense SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graphs, then merged pairwise into a single graph. Every chunk-level solve is independent, which is what the design intended to parallelize across the cloud.

sections.heading: Chunks.
sections.text: The image stream is split by timestamp into disjoint chunks (“sequences”), each a continuous imaging run in which every frame overlaps another frame in the same chunk. Chunks larger than 200 200 frames are subdivided. Chunks are the unit of parallelism.

sections.heading: Intra-sequence PGO.
sections.text: Within a chunk, images are indexed with NetVLAD [ 2 ] in a FAISS [ 7 ] store; each frame retrieves visual neighbors plus GPS-proximate geometric neighbors. Retrieved pairs are matched with SuperPoint [ 6 ] + + LightGlue [ 17 ] , verified against degeneracy (minimum feature motion, essential-vs-homography inlier test, a 3 ∘ 3^{\circ} median-triangulation-angle floor), and reduced to a relative rotation and an up-to-scale translation from the essential matrix [ 18 ] . That translation is scaled by the GPS distance between the two frames. Each verified pair becomes an edge in an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graph solved with g2o [ 14 ] ; the objective is the standard robust sum of relative-pose residuals, E = ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ ℰ ρ ⁡ ( [ log ⁡ ( T j − 1 ​ T j ​ i ​ T i ) ] ∨ ⁣ ⊤ ​ Ω j ​ i ​ [ log ⁡ ( T j − 1 ​ T j ​ i ​ T i ) ] ∨ ) , E=\!\!\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}\!\!\rho\!\left(\big[\log(T_{j}^{-1}T_{ji}T_{i})\big]^{\!\vee\top}\,\Omega_{ji}\,\big[\log(T_{j}^{-1}T_{ji}T_{i})\big]^{\!\vee}\right), (3) with Ω j ​ i \Omega_{ji} a hand-set information matrix (high on rotation, low on translation) and ρ \rho a Huber kernel. Each chunk yields a dense graph in which a frame is tied to about 100 100 others.

sections.heading: Retained bundle adjustment.
sections.text: The pipeline does not end there, and this is the design’s most consequential compromise. Each chunk’s matches are imported into a COLMAP database and a bundle-adjustment pass refines poses, intrinsics, and points. The points that pass triangulates are then reused: they are what the 3 3 D– 2 2 D constraints below are built from. BA is thus removed only globally . It is not run over the full capture, which is where the cost argument of Sec. 1 bites, but it survives inside every chunk, and structure survives with it. The system is accordingly BA-reduced, not BA-free, and we return in Sec. 5.4 to why the pure-pose design could not shed this last dependency.

sections.heading: Inter-sequence constraints and merge.
sections.text: Chunks are still disconnected. We form a K × K K\times K table whose ( i , j ) (i,j) entry holds cross-chunk constraints, 2 2 D– 2 2 D essential (GPS-scaled) and 3 3 D– 2 2 D perspective- n n -point (PnP) [ 15 ] edges, the latter resolved against the per-chunk BA points; 3 3 D– 3 3 D point-cloud alignment was tried and abandoned as unstable. The final stage greedily merges the pair of chunks with the most constraints: a robust SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) average of the pairwise relative transforms (iterated 3 ​ σ 3\sigma rejection) pre-aligns one chunk to the other, g2o re-optimizes with the cross-chunk edges enabled, and the two chunks collapse into one. This repeats until a single graph remains. Information matrices encode trust: PnP edges 7 × 7\times essential edges, intra-sequence edges up-weighted 10 × 10\times before the merge.

sections.heading: Intended parallelism.
sections.text: Every intra-sequence solve is independent and each K × K K\times K entry is independent, so the front end is designed to run across a cloud cluster.

sections.heading: 4 Outcomes
sections.text: We evaluated the pipeline internally on 40 40 proprietary drone scenes. Across the set it neither beats COLMAP nor yields metrics useful on their own, so we do not tabulate aggregate numbers that would only restate a uniform shortfall. Instead we elucidate two representative self-captured scenes (houses of 824 824 and 741 741 frames) in detail: precisely because they neither beat COLMAP nor behave anomalously, they make a clean test bed for reasoning about why a pose-only, structure-free formulation falls short. We compare against a tuned COLMAP baseline (GPU extraction and matching, vocab-tree matcher, hierarchical mapper), and add the public GauU-Scene V2 [ 25 ] drone dataset with lidar ground truth. Tabs. 1 and 2 collect the numbers and Fig. 3 shows a representative splat pair. The poses agree with COLMAP to 0.5 0.5 – 0.6 ∘ 0.6^{\circ} and to within about 2 2 m, in a space where the trajectories themselves span more than 100 100 m, and the splats are recognizable ( Fig. 4 ). Of the two axes the system was built to win, speed and splat quality, the outcome is split. It has real potential to beat COLMAP on speed: the parallel time beats COLMAP by a wide margin. But we had no incentive to pursue that implementation with full vigor, because the splat quality was never comparable to what COLMAP poses produce. On the external dataset one scene failed outright and the rest contained large outliers, though we do report the median here. Sec. 5 explains why each of these follows from the method’s design. sections.heading: 5 Why the method fails
sections.text: We give four causes, each supported by the system’s own design and measurements. They are not of one kind, and separating them matters for how much the reader should conclude. Two are representational : they follow from what a pose-only formulation can express, hold for any parameter setting, and are argued below from the structure of the estimator rather than from our numbers. SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges have no scale degree of freedom ( Sec. 5.2 ), and a two-view edge cannot encode the simultaneous coupling that one point observed in many views imposes ( Sec. 5.4 ). No information matrix, merge order, or initialization repairs either; they bound what the formulation can do. The other two are implementation choices of this pipeline: sequence-wise ordering and merging ( Sec. 5.3 ) and reliance on consumer GPS as the metric ruler ( Sec. 5.5 ), together with the hand-set information matrices of Sec. 5.6 . Better choices exist for each, and we say so as we go. The honest limit of our evidence is the boundary between these two kinds. Since we ablate none of the four, the analysis locates where a ceiling comes from without showing that our measurements sit at it rather than at a lower floor set by the implementation; a better-engineered pose-only pipeline should beat the numbers in Sec. 4 , perhaps substantially. What it cannot do is escape the two representational limits, and Sec. 6 is written for whoever tries. The poses are close to COLMAP and the splat is recognizable; the failures analyzed below are quality and consistency gaps, not gross breakage.

sections.heading: 5.1 Runtime is not where the method fails
sections.text: The founding motivation was a runtime argument, and on its own terms it is sound. The cost splits into two parts that scale very differently. The matching front end, per frame, NetVLAD retrieval, SuperPoint + + LightGlue against about 100 100 neighbors, and two-view verification of each pair, is the dominant absolute cost, but it is embarrassingly parallel : every pair is matched and verified independently, so it shards trivially across a cloud fleet and imposes no fundamental serial bottleneck. What does not parallelize is the solver , the global optimization that ties the frames into one consistent model, and that is the fundamental bottleneck a distributable pipeline must attack. Reducing it is exactly what a pose-only formulation sets out to do: shrink the per-step system to the six-DoF cameras ( Eq. 2 ) and solve each chunk independently, making the one part that cannot be parallelized as small and as decomposable as possible. In that sense the design targets the right cost. The single-machine (sequential) runtime in Tab. 1 does not beat COLMAP , but the parallel time does. Speed, then, is not where this method fails; its failures, examined next, are geometric.

sections.heading: 5.2 SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges cannot represent scale, so merged sub-maps drift
sections.text: This is the deepest failure. Each intra-sequence graph is metric only up to the GPS scaling applied to its essential-matrix translations, and different chunks acquire slightly different effective scales because their GPS baselines and triangulation geometry differ. The merge then aligns chunks with an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) transform, and Eq. 3 lives entirely in SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) , which has no scale degree of freedom . When two chunks disagree on scale by even a few percent, an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) alignment cannot reconcile them: it trades the error into translation and leaves a residual the optimizer cannot drive to zero. The visible symptom is blur and ghosting at the seams of the merged splat ( Fig. 3 b), and it contributes to the 1.7 1.7 – 2.7 2.7 dB PSNR deficit in Tab. 1 , alongside the GPS noise and weighting choices discussed below, which our measurements cannot separate from it. The argument does not need the attribution: the limitation is visible in the state space itself, before any measurement. Bundle adjustment never encounters this, because 3D points shared across overlapping views implicitly tie their scales together. A pose graph in SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) discards that coupling and has no other mechanism to recover it, so scale drift across merges is not a bug to be tuned away; it is unrepresentable in the chosen state space. Figure 5 : Camera centers, PGO versus COLMAP , both aligned to the GPS metric frame (house 2, 741 741 images, a 148 148 m scene with 104 104 m of vertical ascent). Left: the two sets of centers overlaid. Right: every frame that disagrees by more than 1 1 m is highlighted in color, the rest green. The disagreement is pervasive, 90 % 90\% of frames exceed 1 1 m (median 1.2 1.2 m), and worst on the vertical-ascent frames, up to 29 29 m. The two regimes fail differently: the near-linear ascent trajectories suffer nadir degeneracies, while the rest of the scene inherits scaling error from noisy GPS, either way enough to soften the PGO splat relative to COLMAP . Restoring the missing degree of freedom does not rescue the result, and we tried: lifting each merge to Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) , which does carry a scale term. Such a merge must estimate one similarity ( s , R , t ) (s,R,t) per sequence boundary from the inter-sequence constraints alone, and with few, wide-baseline shared observations that estimate starts far from its optimum. Compounding this, the GPS-derived constraints conflict : each pulls the boundary toward a different, meter-scale, anisotropically noisy anchor, so the solve settles at a compromise satisfying none of them, metrically plausible but still blurring the seam. The missing scale degree of freedom is therefore necessary but not sufficient. Under a sequential merge this conflict is structural rather than an artifact of noise levels, and seeing why shows exactly where Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) alone relocates the problem instead of removing it. Scaling an entire sequence together with all of its pose constraints does keep that sequence internally consistent, so once we scale sequence 2 2 to agree with sequence 1 1 the pair ( 1 , 2 ) (1,2) is mutually consistent, and every inter-sequence constraint incident on 2 2 is scaled to match. An astute reader might expect this rescaling to be absorbed automatically as the next sequence is merged. It is not. When a third sequence is merged against the first two, the inter-pose constraints → 1 3\!\to\!1 and → 2 3\!\to\!2 both carry the raw GPS scale, because that is how sequence 3 3 was reconstructed. But sequence 2 2 has already been rescaled to match 1 1 , so → 1 3\!\to\!1 is roughly consistent up to ordinary scale drift while → 2 3\!\to\!2 disagrees by exactly the correction we applied to 2 2 . The optimizer is handed two contradictory statements about the same scale, and no single scalar satisfies both. The similarity that resolved ( 1 , 2 ) (1,2) thus reappears as a fresh conflict at 3 3 : Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) shifts the scale mismatch along the merge order rather than removing it.

sections.heading: Multi-way synchronization was not attempted.
sections.text: The contradiction above arises only because the merges happen one after another : each merge aligns the incoming chunk to the partial map so far, so by chunk 3 3 , chunk 2 2 has already been corrected by its merge with 1 1 while chunk 3 3 still carries raw GPS scale. That mismatch, not Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) itself, is what no single scalar can satisfy. The alternative is to estimate all K K chunk similarities at once from the full graph of inter-chunk constraints, so no chunk is corrected before the others are accounted for. We did not try it. Such multi-way Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) synchronization, in the spirit of motion and rotation averaging [ 10 , 12 ] and similarity synchronization [ 3 ] , spreads inconsistent pairwise scales in a least-squares sense over all chunks. The scale component in particular is a linear problem, which is what makes this attractive. Give chunk k k an unknown log-scale σ k = log ⁡ s k \sigma_{k}=\log s_{k} ; each cross-chunk constraint between i i and j j measures a ratio s i ​ j s_{ij} and so contributes one equation σ j − σ i = log ⁡ s i ​ j \sigma_{j}-\sigma_{i}=\log s_{ij} . Over the populated entries of the K × K K\times K table these stack into an overdetermined linear system in K K unknowns whose normal equations are a weighted graph Laplacian, determined up to a single global gauge that GPS, or fixing one chunk, supplies. Rotations follow by rotation averaging and translations are linear once scales and rotations are known, the standard Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) synchronization recipe [ 3 ] . Crucially, every chunk’s scale is then set by all of its constraints simultaneously, so a disagreement between → 1 3\!\to\!1 and → 2 3\!\to\!2 is distributed as residual rather than resolved in favour of whichever merge happened first. With K K in the tens the solve is negligible beside the matching front end, so it costs nothing the speed argument cares about. We expect this to reduce the seam error materially and regard it as the most promising untried repair, though it redistributes inconsistency rather than supplying the absolute scale the capture lacks.

sections.heading:
5.3 Sequence-by-sequence ordering leaves sub-maps ill-conditioned before
they merge
sections.text: This cause and the two that follow are implementation choices, each of which could have been made differently and none of which we ablated. They are worth recording because the divide-and-merge decomposition that makes a pose-only design attractive to parallelize is exactly what makes them tempting. The pipeline orders images by capture sequence, solves each sequence independently, and only then merges, and the ordering itself is a failure mode, for two compounding reasons. First, some sequences are geometrically degenerate in isolation : a nadir ascent, where the drone rises vertically over a fixed point, supplies almost no translational parallax, so the sub-map is fundamentally unconstrained up to the missing baseline. Solved alone, it has no way to recover the structure a neighbouring oblique sequence would have supplied. Second, to absorb the meter-scale GPS noise each sequence settles into its own local optimum that best trades its observations against its noisy anchors. Because every sub-map made that trade independently, the local optima disagree; when the sequences merge, the cross-sequence constraints are in large mutual conflict , far outside the basin the merge can reconcile, and the global solve settles at a sub-optimal compromise. The lesson is about ordering, not merging: an image ordering that proceeds strictly sequence-by-sequence guarantees these isolated, separately-converged pieces, and no merge strategy applied afterwards can undo a sub-map that has already converged to the wrong basin. An ideal ordering would never take one sequence to convergence in isolation. Interleaving images across sequences from the start, so that cross-sequence constraints shape each pose before it commits to a local optimum, keeps the whole capture in a single jointly constrained basin rather than assembling it from pre-settled, mutually inconsistent parts, and it costs nothing in parallelism: the chunking that makes the front end shardable is independent of the order in which poses are allowed to influence one another. We did not build that ordering, so we cannot say how much of the merge conflict it would remove; it is the ablation we would run first.

sections.heading: 5.4 Removing shared structure removes multi-view consistency
sections.text: The premise was that pose-only optimization could reach BA-grade quality. But the thing that makes BA’s poses globally consistent is precisely the structure the method discards: a 3D point observed in many frames forces those frames to agree, and BA averages their independent measurement errors into one consistent estimate. A pose graph of pairwise relative transforms has no such shared latent variable; it is only as good as its edges, and edge errors accumulate rather than cancel. Two facts in the system confirm that this coupling could not simply be dropped. First, the pipeline still runs a per-chunk COLMAP bundle adjustment, and the 3 3 D– 2 2 D PnP constraints that stitch chunks are derived from the points that BA produced, so structure was reintroduced through the back door. This cuts two ways, and we state both. It is the clearest evidence that the coupling is load-bearing: the design reached for structure exactly where pose-only constraints proved too weak to stitch sub-maps, and no version of the pipeline ran without it. But it also means we never put the pure-pose premise fully on trial, and our negative result is correspondingly bounded. What we have shown to fail is pose-only estimation at the global scale , with BA still supporting each chunk from below; a formulation that removed BA entirely would inherit every weakness catalogued here and lose that support besides, so we expect it to fare worse, but we did not measure it. Second, the one path that tried to use structure-to-structure information directly, the 3 3 D– 3 3 D point-cloud alignment edge, was abandoned as unstable. That instability is no accident: projectively triangulated points carry an uncertainty that grows with observation distance and shrinks with disparity, so a point seen from 50 50 m away is localized far more loosely than one seen from a few meters. A point-cloud alignment that treats every point as equally certain then forces such a loosely-triangulated far point, from one sequence, to line up precisely with a tightly-triangulated near point of the same structure from another; without propagating those per-point uncertainties into the cost, the solve trades a well-localized constraint against a badly-localized one and settles at a poorly-converged compromise. The method’s own choices show that without shared structure the estimate is not consistent enough, and with it the “BA-free” claim no longer holds.

sections.heading: 5.5 Consumer GPS is a noisy ruler, not an anchor
sections.text: GPS plays an outsized role: it is the only metric signal, used to scale each pairwise translation and to select neighbors, yet it enters only as a relative ruler on translations, never as a soft absolute position prior on the nodes. So nothing pins global scale or arrests drift; each chunk’s scale floats independently, exactly the freedom Sec. 5.2 cannot later remove. Worse, the ruler itself is imprecise. These drones carry consumer-grade GNSS (GPS). With an RTK fix the receiver is accurate to a few centimeters, but the captures rarely hold an RTK lock, and without it horizontal position is off by 0.5 0.5 – 1.0 1.0 m. That error does not stay contained: fed in as the scale of every essential-matrix translation, it is large relative to the inter-frame baselines it scales, injecting meter-scale noise into precisely the SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) translations the merge already cannot correct. Altitude is worse still: on several of these drones the vertical channel comes from a barometric altimeter, so the relative- Z Z component carries far more uncertainty than the horizontal ones. Feeding a strongly anisotropic , meter-scale, sometimes-biased position signal into an optimizer that treats it as a metric constraint makes the pose graph ill-posed, though not uniformly. The circular orbit sequences are largely safe: their wide, multi-directional baselines triangulate structure, and vertical scale with it, from the imagery. The damage concentrates on the nadir sequences , the near-straight vertical ascents flown looking straight down, where the geometry is degenerate: straight-line motion gives no cross-baseline, and the nadir view aligns the poorly-triangulated depth axis with the vertical, so “the camera climbed” and “the scene grew” are nearly indistinguishable. Vertical scale is then only weakly constrained: the nadir edges resist it little, and the one term that penalizes a wrong vertical scale, the barometric- Z Z prior, is too noisy to push back. With so little curvature there, Eq. 3 is nearly flat, so the estimate can drift far at almost no cost. This is a direct source of the large outliers and outright failure we observed ( Tab. 2 ). A pose-only formulation has no shared structure to fall back on when its metric signal is this noisy; bundle adjustment derives scale from the imagery itself and needs GPS only as a weak gauge, so the same fix does it little harm.

sections.heading: 5.6 Trust is hand-set, not propagated
sections.text: Compounding the noise, every constraint’s influence is a hand-chosen information matrix (rotation over translation, PnP 7 × 7\times essential, refined edges 10 × 10\times ) rather than a value propagated from the data’s uncertainty. Without a data-driven model, a triangulation-noisy or badly-GPS-scaled match cannot be down-weighted against a clean one, the mechanical reason the 3 3 D– 3 3 D constraint was unusable and the reason the same fixed weights that worked on the tuning scenes produced large outliers and an outright failure (HAV) on a capture whose noise profile differed. Stability resting on manually balanced trust, over a signal as heteroscedastic as consumer GPS, does not transfer. This is the most fixable of the four causes and the one that most confounds our results: with no learned-weight configuration run, we cannot separate error from the formulation from error from weighting it badly.

sections.heading: 6 Lessons
sections.text: The causes above translate into concrete guidance for anyone drawn to the same shortcut, replacing structure-aware optimization with a cheaper pose-only surrogate on structured captures. 1. Two independent speedups, and the front end is the bigger one. Dropping the points for a structure-less, pose-only optimization is genuinely faster than a full bundle adjustment: it removes the most expensive part of the solve, and that saving is real and worth taking. The larger opportunity, though, is the matching front end that dominates absolute cost. It is embarrassingly parallel and shards cleanly across workers, and the levers that matter there are mundane, the retrieval budget per frame, pruning pairs before verification, and GPU-parallel extraction and matching. Both are worth accelerating, but the front end’s gains are far easier to capture, because they come from trivial parallelism rather than from reformulating the estimator, and reformulating the estimator is what costs accuracy. 2. If you drop the points, add scale back explicitly. BA’s hidden gift is that shared structure couples the scales of overlapping views. A pose-only formulation must recover that coupling elsewhere, through Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) edges and a Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) merge estimated jointly over all sub-maps rather than pairwise ( Sec. 5.2 ). SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graphs across independently-scaled sub-maps are a scale trap. 3. Use GPS as an absolute prior, not merely a ruler, but model its noise. A soft absolute position constraint on every node pins global scale and arrests drift. It helps only if weighted by its true, anisotropic uncertainty, looser in barometric Z Z than in the horizontal plane and looser still without an RTK lock, otherwise the meter-scale error re-enters as bias. 4. Keep a little structure. A pose graph with zero shared 3D points is on the wrong side of a cliff. Retaining even a small point set, a few times the camera count rather than the hundreds-of-times BA carries, restores multi-view consistency while keeping the problem small, the structured-but-lean middle, not pure PGO, the cost argument should have pointed to. 5. Propagate uncertainty; do not hand-tune it. Data-driven information matrices are what make structure-to-structure constraints usable. Fixed trust ratios are a liability that grows with capture diversity.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We asked whether, in the dense loop-closure regime splatting captures uniquely provide, pose-graph optimization could displace bundle adjustment as the estimation objective. For the system we built the answer is no, twice over: it did not match COLMAP ’s accuracy, and it did not even dispense with BA to get there, keeping a per-chunk pass whose triangulated points its own cross-chunk constraints are built on. The causes divide, and the division is the point. Some are ours to own: a consumer-GPS anchor too noisy and too anisotropic to hold scale, greedy pairwise merging, sequence-by-sequence ordering, and hand-set information matrices. Each is a repairable engineering decision we did not ablate, and a careful reimplementation should beat our numbers. Two causes are not repairable that way. The SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) state space cannot represent the scale differences its own GPS-scaled sub-maps introduce, whatever weights the edges carry; and a graph of two-view edges cannot reconstitute the many-view coupling that gives bundle adjustment its consistency. These are properties of the formulation, not settings within it, and they are what a future design has to answer for: Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) constraints estimated jointly rather than pairwise, absolute uncertainty-aware GPS priors, and a thin layer of retained structure. How much of the measured gap those limits account for would take the ablations we did not run; we hope the account still saves the next team the same detour.

sections.heading: When the approach might be worth revisiting.
sections.text: Several failures trace to the noisy metric anchor, not the formulation. Under an RTK fix, position is accurate to a few centimetres in all of ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) , enough to pin scale across merges and stop inter-sequence constraints conflicting at the meter scale. A lightweight distributed pose graph, with a few sparse retained points supplying the coupling pure SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) / Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) edges cannot, would then deserve a fresh attempt: the negative result is a scoping one, pose-only, GPS-scaled estimation is the wrong tool for consumer -grade capture.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.14090v1 [cs.RO] 08 Oct 2026 When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting Senthil Palanisamy Azwad Sabik Alan Dolhasz Mira Slavcheva Affiliation: Matterport Abstract Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing : it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure , not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting. Keywords: Pose estimation Gaussian splatting Pose graph optimization Failure analysis Structure from motion 1 Introduction Gaussian splatting [ 13 ] has made high-quality novel-view synthesis of real scenes routine, and with it the need for accurate camera poses at scale. The default recipe passes images through a structure-from-motion (SfM) system, almost always COLMAP [ 21 ] , before training. For large exterior scenes this SfM step is the bottleneck: robust incremental reconstruction of thousands of drone frames can take hours. The captures used for exterior splatting are, however, far from the “images-in-the-wild” regime SfM is built for: as above, a home is flown as several dense overlapping orbits, every frame carries GPS, and consecutive frames overlap strongly. It is natural to ask whether this structure lets us avoid the expensive part of SfM. Bundle adjustment [ 23 ] jointly refines camera poses and a large point cloud, its cost nominally dominated by the points: each 3D point adds three parameters and there are far more points than cameras. If we could constrain the cameras directly , through a dense graph of pairwise relative-pose measurements, the optimization would touch only the six degrees of freedom per camera and be both smaller and trivially decomposable per sequence. This intuition can be sharpened, and it is what makes a pose-only formulation tempting rather than naive. Each Gauss–Newton step of bundle adjustment [ 9 ] solves a normal-equation system that, with the camera update Δ ​ 𝐱 c \Delta\mathbf{x}_{c} ordered above the landmark update Δ ​ 𝐱 p \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p} , takes the block form [ B E E ⊤ C ] ​ [ Δ ​ 𝐱 c Δ ​ 𝐱 p ] = [ 𝐯 𝐰 ] , \begin{bmatrix}B&E\\ E^{\top}&C\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}\\ \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{v}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}, (1) with a camera block B B , a landmark block C C , and their coupling E E . Because C C carries one 3 × 3 3\times 3 diagonal block per 3D point it is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, so BA does not in fact pay for the landmarks directly: it eliminates Δ ​ 𝐱 p \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p} by the Schur complement, left-multiplying Eq. 1 by [ I − E ​ C − 1 0 I ] \left[\begin{smallmatrix}I&-EC^{-1}\\ 0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right] to reach the much smaller, pose-only reduced system ( B − E ​ C − 1 ​ E ⊤ ) ⏟ S ​ Δ ​ 𝐱 c = 𝐯 − E ​ C − 1 ​ 𝐰 , \underbrace{\big(B-EC^{-1}E^{\top}\big)}_{\textstyle S}\,\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}=\mathbf{v}-EC^{-1}\mathbf{w}, (2) and only then back-substitutes Δ ​ 𝐱 p = C − 1 ​ ( 𝐰 − E ⊤ ​ Δ ​ 𝐱 c ) \Delta\mathbf{x}_{p}=C^{-1}(\mathbf{w}-E^{\top}\Delta\mathbf{x}_{c}) . Forming the reduction and back-substituting are redone at every iteration, so the dominant work is the repeated solve of S S , not the landmarks. If BA’s expensive core is already a pose-only system, the attractive idea is to build S S directly , as a pose graph of relative-pose constraints, skipping the landmark bookkeeping and marginalization altogether and arriving at the reduced system for free ( Fig. 1 ). The core question is whether the S S that pose-graph optimization assembles directly approaches the S S that BA produces by marginalization, in the limit of increasingly many inter-frame constraints. Figure 1 : The pose-only intuition. Bundle adjustment (left) couples the camera poses to a large landmark cloud through observation edges. Because the landmark block C C is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, BA marginalizes the landmarks via the Schur complement into a much smaller, pose-only reduced system S = B − E ​ C − 1 ​ E ⊤ S=B-EC^{-1}E^{\top} (right), solves it for the poses, and only then back-substitutes for the points. Since BA’s expensive core is already this pose-only system, a pose-only formulation tries to assemble S S directly from inter-pose relative-pose constraints (dashed), skipping the landmark detour. Both routes target the same S S ; this paper asks whether the shortcut recovers bundle-adjustment-grade poses. There is a further, more principled reason to study this here. Pose-graph optimization is a mature and well-understood tool [ 11 ] , but in robotics and SLAM [ 4 ] it is almost always a back-end refinement : a front end (visual odometry or SLAM) first produces poses of reasonable accuracy, and PGO then uses loop-closure edges to redistribute the accumulated drift into a globally consistent trajectory. Its power grows with the number and diversity of those loop closures. Splatting captures sit at an extreme of that regime: because the imagery is so dense, essentially every frame closes loops with dozens of others, so the pose graph is far richer than the sparse loop-closure graphs PGO is usually handed. This invites a genuine research question, in the limit of an ever-denser loop-closure graph, does pose-only optimization converge to bundle-adjustment accuracy? If it did, the dense structure of splatting captures would be exactly the setting in which to trade BA for PGO. We treat answering this, empirically and then structurally, as the study’s core purpose. This is the hypothesis we set out to validate: that dense pose-graph optimization, used not as a post-hoc SLAM refinement but as the primary estimation objective, can recover poses of BA-grade quality on these structured, GPS-tagged drone captures , faster and in a cloud-parallel form . We built the system and ran it on self-captured drone scenes and a public benchmark. The strong form of the hypothesis proved false. This paper explains why, using the system’s own design and numbers, and is careful about which parts of the explanation generalize: two of the causes are properties of the pose-only formulation that no parameter setting escapes, while the rest are choices this pipeline made and a better one could revisit. We keep the two apart throughout ( Sec. 5 ). We recall the related landscape ( Sec. 2 ), the pipeline ( Sec. 3 ) and its outcomes ( Sec. 4 ), then give the methodological failure analysis that is our contribution ( Sec. 5 ) and the design lessons it implies ( Sec. 6 ). 2 Related work COLMAP [ 21 ] is the de facto general-purpose standard for pose estimation in vision and the default front end for splatting. We do not aim to replace it there: we target only the narrow, structured regime of exterior splatting captures, using COLMAP as the reference a specialized pose-only design must match. GLOMAP [ 19 ] showed that global SfM can approach incremental accuracy at lower cost, yet COLMAP remains the method of choice when robust registration is required. Theia [ 22 ] offers both incremental and global SfM but is chiefly a researcher’s toolkit. Learned, feed-forward estimators such as VGGT [ 24 ] and Depth-Anything-3 [ 16 ] predict poses, depth and intrinsics in a single pass and are advancing quickly. They make excellent one-shot pose initializers, but as we confirm below they have not yet reached the pose accuracy of a robust system that nonlinearly refines poses. Our matching front end follows hierarchical localization [ 20 ] , pairing SuperPoint features [ 6 ] with LightGlue [ 17 ] and NetVLAD [ 2 ] retrieval indexed with FAISS [ 7 ] , a modern replacement for bag-of-words retrieval [ 8 ] . Distributing SfM across machines dates back to Building Rome in a Day [ 1 ] . Our design differs in demoting bundle adjustment [ 23 ] from the global objective to a per-chunk step and making pose-graph optimization carry the estimation, solved with g2o [ 14 ] (GTSAM [ 5 ] is the common alternative), and in exploiting GPS and sequential capture. It is the limits of that partial substitution, and of the pure-pose formulation it approximates, that we analyze. 3 The system we built We summarize the pipeline only enough to make the analysis precise. It is not a general-purpose SfM system but one built expressly around the structure of these captures, dense sequential overlap, per-frame GPS, and multi-orbit coverage; a three-stage divide–compute–merge design ( Fig. 2 ). Figure 2 : System overview. The image stream is split into per-sequence chunks that are optimized independently as dense SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graphs, then merged pairwise into a single graph. Every chunk-level solve is independent, which is what the design intended to parallelize across the cloud. Chunks. The image stream is split by timestamp into disjoint chunks (“sequences”), each a continuous imaging run in which every frame overlaps another frame in the same chunk. Chunks larger than 200 200 frames are subdivided. Chunks are the unit of parallelism. Intra-sequence PGO. Within a chunk, images are indexed with NetVLAD [ 2 ] in a FAISS [ 7 ] store; each frame retrieves visual neighbors plus GPS-proximate geometric neighbors. Retrieved pairs are matched with SuperPoint [ 6 ] + + LightGlue [ 17 ] , verified against degeneracy (minimum feature motion, essential-vs-homography inlier test, a 3 ∘ 3^{\circ} median-triangulation-angle floor), and reduced to a relative rotation and an up-to-scale translation from the essential matrix [ 18 ] . That translation is scaled by the GPS distance between the two frames. Each verified pair becomes an edge in an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graph solved with g2o [ 14 ] ; the objective is the standard robust sum of relative-pose residuals, E = ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ ℰ ρ ⁡ ( [ log ⁡ ( T j − 1 ​ T j ​ i ​ T i ) ] ∨ ⁣ ⊤ ​ Ω j ​ i ​ [ log ⁡ ( T j − 1 ​ T j ​ i ​ T i ) ] ∨ ) , E=\!\!\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}\!\!\rho\!\left(\big[\log(T_{j}^{-1}T_{ji}T_{i})\big]^{\!\vee\top}\,\Omega_{ji}\,\big[\log(T_{j}^{-1}T_{ji}T_{i})\big]^{\!\vee}\right), (3) with Ω j ​ i \Omega_{ji} a hand-set information matrix (high on rotation, low on translation) and ρ \rho a Huber kernel. Each chunk yields a dense graph in which a frame is tied to about 100 100 others. Retained bundle adjustment. The pipeline does not end there, and this is the design’s most consequential compromise. Each chunk’s matches are imported into a COLMAP database and a bundle-adjustment pass refines poses, intrinsics, and points. The points that pass triangulates are then reused: they are what the 3 3 D– 2 2 D constraints below are built from. BA is thus removed only globally . It is not run over the full capture, which is where the cost argument of Sec. 1 bites, but it survives inside every chunk, and structure survives with it. The system is accordingly BA-reduced, not BA-free, and we return in Sec. 5.4 to why the pure-pose design could not shed this last dependency. Inter-sequence constraints and merge. Chunks are still disconnected. We form a K × K K\times K table whose ( i , j ) (i,j) entry holds cross-chunk constraints, 2 2 D– 2 2 D essential (GPS-scaled) and 3 3 D– 2 2 D perspective- n n -point (PnP) [ 15 ] edges, the latter resolved against the per-chunk BA points; 3 3 D– 3 3 D point-cloud alignment was tried and abandoned as unstable. The final stage greedily merges the pair of chunks with the most constraints: a robust SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) average of the pairwise relative transforms (iterated 3 ​ σ 3\sigma rejection) pre-aligns one chunk to the other, g2o re-optimizes with the cross-chunk edges enabled, and the two chunks collapse into one. This repeats until a single graph remains. Information matrices encode trust: PnP edges 7 × 7\times essential edges, intra-sequence edges up-weighted 10 × 10\times before the merge. Intended parallelism. Every intra-sequence solve is independent and each K × K K\times K entry is independent, so the front end is designed to run across a cloud cluster. 4 Outcomes We evaluated the pipeline internally on 40 40 proprietary drone scenes. Across the set it neither beats COLMAP nor yields metrics useful on their own, so we do not tabulate aggregate numbers that would only restate a uniform shortfall. Instead we elucidate two representative self-captured scenes (houses of 824 824 and 741 741 frames) in detail: precisely because they neither beat COLMAP nor behave anomalously, they make a clean test bed for reasoning about why a pose-only, structure-free formulation falls short. We compare against a tuned COLMAP baseline (GPU extraction and matching, vocab-tree matcher, hierarchical mapper), and add the public GauU-Scene V2 [ 25 ] drone dataset with lidar ground truth. Tabs. 1 and 2 collect the numbers and Fig. 3 shows a representative splat pair. The poses agree with COLMAP to 0.5 0.5 – 0.6 ∘ 0.6^{\circ} and to within about 2 2 m, in a space where the trajectories themselves span more than 100 100 m, and the splats are recognizable ( Fig. 4 ). Of the two axes the system was built to win, speed and splat quality, the outcome is split. It has real potential to beat COLMAP on speed: the parallel time beats COLMAP by a wide margin. But we had no incentive to pursue that implementation with full vigor, because the splat quality was never comparable to what COLMAP poses produce. On the external dataset one scene failed outright and the rest contained large outliers, though we do report the median here. Sec. 5 explains why each of these follows from the method’s design. They are not of one kind, and separating them matters for how much the reader should conclude. Two are representational : they follow from what a pose-only formulation can express, hold for any parameter setting, and are argued below from the structure of the estimator rather than from our numbers. SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges have no scale degree of freedom ( Sec. 5.2 ), and a two-view edge cannot encode the simultaneous coupling that one point observed in many views imposes ( Sec. 5.4 ). No information matrix, merge order, or initialization repairs either; they bound what the formulation can do. The other two are implementation choices of this pipeline: sequence-wise ordering and merging ( Sec. 5.3 ) and reliance on consumer GPS as the metric ruler ( Sec. 5.5 ), together with the hand-set information matrices of Sec. 5.6 . Better choices exist for each, and we say so as we go. The honest limit of our evidence is the boundary between these two kinds. Since we ablate none of the four, the analysis locates where a ceiling comes from without showing that our measurements sit at it rather than at a lower floor set by the implementation; a better-engineered pose-only pipeline should beat the numbers in Sec. 4 , perhaps substantially. What it cannot do is escape the two representational limits, and Sec. 6 is written for whoever tries. (a) estimated camera poses (b) Gaussian-splat reconstruction Figure 4 : Qualitative output of the pose-only pipeline on a self-captured house: (a) the camera poses it estimates and (b) the resulting Gaussian-splat reconstruction. The poses are close to COLMAP and the splat is recognizable; the failures analyzed below are quality and consistency gaps, not gross breakage. 5.1 Runtime is not where the method fails The founding motivation was a runtime argument, and on its own terms it is sound. The cost splits into two parts that scale very differently. The matching front end, per frame, NetVLAD retrieval, SuperPoint + + LightGlue against about 100 100 neighbors, and two-view verification of each pair, is the dominant absolute cost, but it is embarrassingly parallel : every pair is matched and verified independently, so it shards trivially across a cloud fleet and imposes no fundamental serial bottleneck. What does not parallelize is the solver , the global optimization that ties the frames into one consistent model, and that is the fundamental bottleneck a distributable pipeline must attack. Reducing it is exactly what a pose-only formulation sets out to do: shrink the per-step system to the six-DoF cameras ( Eq. 2 ) and solve each chunk independently, making the one part that cannot be parallelized as small and as decomposable as possible. In that sense the design targets the right cost. The single-machine (sequential) runtime in Tab. 1 does not beat COLMAP , but the parallel time does. Speed, then, is not where this method fails; its failures, examined next, are geometric. 5.2 SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) edges cannot represent scale, so merged sub-maps drift This is the deepest failure. Each intra-sequence graph is metric only up to the GPS scaling applied to its essential-matrix translations, and different chunks acquire slightly different effective scales because their GPS baselines and triangulation geometry differ. The merge then aligns chunks with an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) transform, and Eq. 3 lives entirely in SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) , which has no scale degree of freedom . When two chunks disagree on scale by even a few percent, an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) alignment cannot reconcile them: it trades the error into translation and leaves a residual the optimizer cannot drive to zero. The visible symptom is blur and ghosting at the seams of the merged splat ( Fig. 3 b), and it contributes to the 1.7 1.7 – 2.7 2.7 dB PSNR deficit in Tab. 1 , alongside the GPS noise and weighting choices discussed below, which our measurements cannot separate from it. The argument does not need the attribution: the limitation is visible in the state space itself, before any measurement. Bundle adjustment never encounters this, because 3D points shared across overlapping views implicitly tie their scales together. A pose graph in SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) discards that coupling and has no other mechanism to recover it, so scale drift across merges is not a bug to be tuned away; it is unrepresentable in the chosen state space. They are worth recording because the divide-and-merge decomposition that makes a pose-only design attractive to parallelize is exactly what makes them tempting. The pipeline orders images by capture sequence, solves each sequence independently, and only then merges, and the ordering itself is a failure mode, for two compounding reasons. First, some sequences are geometrically degenerate in isolation : a nadir ascent, where the drone rises vertically over a fixed point, supplies almost no translational parallax, so the sub-map is fundamentally unconstrained up to the missing baseline. Solved alone, it has no way to recover the structure a neighbouring oblique sequence would have supplied. Second, to absorb the meter-scale GPS noise each sequence settles into its own local optimum that best trades its observations against its noisy anchors. Because every sub-map made that trade independently, the local optima disagree; when the sequences merge, the cross-sequence constraints are in large mutual conflict , far outside the basin the merge can reconcile, and the global solve settles at a sub-optimal compromise. The lesson is about ordering, not merging: an image ordering that proceeds strictly sequence-by-sequence guarantees these isolated, separately-converged pieces, and no merge strategy applied afterwards can undo a sub-map that has already converged to the wrong basin. An ideal ordering would never take one sequence to convergence in isolation. Interleaving images across sequences from the start, so that cross-sequence constraints shape each pose before it commits to a local optimum, keeps the whole capture in a single jointly constrained basin rather than assembling it from pre-settled, mutually inconsistent parts, and it costs nothing in parallelism: the chunking that makes the front end shardable is independent of the order in which poses are allowed to influence one another. We did not build that ordering, so we cannot say how much of the merge conflict it would remove; it is the ablation we would run first. 5.4 Removing shared structure removes multi-view consistency The premise was that pose-only optimization could reach BA-grade quality. But the thing that makes BA’s poses globally consistent is precisely the structure the method discards: a 3D point observed in many frames forces those frames to agree, and BA averages their independent measurement errors into one consistent estimate. A pose graph of pairwise relative transforms has no such shared latent variable; it is only as good as its edges, and edge errors accumulate rather than cancel. Two facts in the system confirm that this coupling could not simply be dropped. First, the pipeline still runs a per-chunk COLMAP bundle adjustment, and the 3 3 D– 2 2 D PnP constraints that stitch chunks are derived from the points that BA produced, so structure was reintroduced through the back door. This cuts two ways, and we state both. It is the clearest evidence that the coupling is load-bearing: the design reached for structure exactly where pose-only constraints proved too weak to stitch sub-maps, and no version of the pipeline ran without it. But it also means we never put the pure-pose premise fully on trial, and our negative result is correspondingly bounded. What we have shown to fail is pose-only estimation at the global scale , with BA still supporting each chunk from below; a formulation that removed BA entirely would inherit every weakness catalogued here and lose that support besides, so we expect it to fare worse, but we did not measure it. Second, the one path that tried to use structure-to-structure information directly, the 3 3 D– 3 3 D point-cloud alignment edge, was abandoned as unstable. That instability is no accident: projectively triangulated points carry an uncertainty that grows with observation distance and shrinks with disparity, so a point seen from 50 50 m away is localized far more loosely than one seen from a few meters. A point-cloud alignment that treats every point as equally certain then forces such a loosely-triangulated far point, from one sequence, to line up precisely with a tightly-triangulated near point of the same structure from another; without propagating those per-point uncertainties into the cost, the solve trades a well-localized constraint against a badly-localized one and settles at a poorly-converged compromise. The method’s own choices show that without shared structure the estimate is not consistent enough, and with it the “BA-free” claim no longer holds. 5.5 Consumer GPS is a noisy ruler, not an anchor GPS plays an outsized role: it is the only metric signal, used to scale each pairwise translation and to select neighbors, yet it enters only as a relative ruler on translations, never as a soft absolute position prior on the nodes. So nothing pins global scale or arrests drift; each chunk’s scale floats independently, exactly the freedom Sec. 5.2 cannot later remove. Worse, the ruler itself is imprecise. These drones carry consumer-grade GNSS (GPS). With an RTK fix the receiver is accurate to a few centimeters, but the captures rarely hold an RTK lock, and without it horizontal position is off by 0.5 0.5 – 1.0 1.0 m. That error does not stay contained: fed in as the scale of every essential-matrix translation, it is large relative to the inter-frame baselines it scales, injecting meter-scale noise into precisely the SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) translations the merge already cannot correct. Altitude is worse still: on several of these drones the vertical channel comes from a barometric altimeter, so the relative- Z Z component carries far more uncertainty than the horizontal ones. Feeding a strongly anisotropic , meter-scale, sometimes-biased position signal into an optimizer that treats it as a metric constraint makes the pose graph ill-posed, though not uniformly. The circular orbit sequences are largely safe: their wide, multi-directional baselines triangulate structure, and vertical scale with it, from the imagery. The damage concentrates on the nadir sequences , the near-straight vertical ascents flown looking straight down, where the geometry is degenerate: straight-line motion gives no cross-baseline, and the nadir view aligns the poorly-triangulated depth axis with the vertical, so “the camera climbed” and “the scene grew” are nearly indistinguishable. Vertical scale is then only weakly constrained: the nadir edges resist it little, and the one term that penalizes a wrong vertical scale, the barometric- Z Z prior, is too noisy to push back. With so little curvature there, Eq. 3 is nearly flat, so the estimate can drift far at almost no cost. This is a direct source of the large outliers and outright failure we observed ( Tab. 2 ). A pose-only formulation has no shared structure to fall back on when its metric signal is this noisy; bundle adjustment derives scale from the imagery itself and needs GPS only as a weak gauge, so the same fix does it little harm. 5.6 Trust is hand-set, not propagated Compounding the noise, every constraint’s influence is a hand-chosen information matrix (rotation over translation, PnP 7 × 7\times essential, refined edges 10 × 10\times ) rather than a value propagated from the data’s uncertainty. Without a data-driven model, a triangulation-noisy or badly-GPS-scaled match cannot be down-weighted against a clean one, the mechanical reason the 3 3 D– 3 3 D constraint was unusable and the reason the same fixed weights that worked on the tuning scenes produced large outliers and an outright failure (HAV) on a capture whose noise profile differed. Stability resting on manually balanced trust, over a signal as heteroscedastic as consumer GPS, does not transfer. This is the most fixable of the four causes and the one that most confounds our results: with no learned-weight configuration run, we cannot separate error from the formulation from error from weighting it badly. 6 Lessons The causes above translate into concrete guidance for anyone drawn to the same shortcut, replacing structure-aware optimization with a cheaper pose-only surrogate on structured captures. 1. Two independent speedups, and the front end is the bigger one. Dropping the points for a structure-less, pose-only optimization is genuinely faster than a full bundle adjustment: it removes the most expensive part of the solve, and that saving is real and worth taking. The larger opportunity, though, is the matching front end that dominates absolute cost. It is embarrassingly parallel and shards cleanly across workers, and the levers that matter there are mundane, the retrieval budget per frame, pruning pairs before verification, and GPU-parallel extraction and matching. Both are worth accelerating, but the front end’s gains are far easier to capture, because they come from trivial parallelism rather than from reformulating the estimator, and reformulating the estimator is what costs accuracy. 2. If you drop the points, add scale back explicitly. BA’s hidden gift is that shared structure couples the scales of overlapping views. A pose-only formulation must recover that coupling elsewhere, through Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) edges and a Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) merge estimated jointly over all sub-maps rather than pairwise ( Sec. 5.2 ). SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose graphs across independently-scaled sub-maps are a scale trap. 3. Use GPS as an absolute prior, not merely a ruler, but model its noise. A soft absolute position constraint on every node pins global scale and arrests drift. It helps only if weighted by its true, anisotropic uncertainty, looser in barometric Z Z than in the horizontal plane and looser still without an RTK lock, otherwise the meter-scale error re-enters as bias. 4. Keep a little structure. A pose graph with zero shared 3D points is on the wrong side of a cliff. Retaining even a small point set, a few times the camera count rather than the hundreds-of-times BA carries, restores multi-view consistency while keeping the problem small, the structured-but-lean middle, not pure PGO, the cost argument should have pointed to. 5. Propagate uncertainty; do not hand-tune it. Data-driven information matrices are what make structure-to-structure constraints usable. Fixed trust ratios are a liability that grows with capture diversity. 7 Conclusion We asked whether, in the dense loop-closure regime splatting captures uniquely provide, pose-graph optimization could displace bundle adjustment as the estimation objective. For the system we built the answer is no, twice over: it did not match COLMAP ’s accuracy, and it did not even dispense with BA to get there, keeping a per-chunk pass whose triangulated points its own cross-chunk constraints are built on. The causes divide, and the division is the point. Some are ours to own: a consumer-GPS anchor too noisy and too anisotropic to hold scale, greedy pairwise merging, sequence-by-sequence ordering, and hand-set information matrices. Each is a repairable engineering decision we did not ablate, and a careful reimplementation should beat our numbers. Two causes are not repairable that way. The SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) state space cannot represent the scale differences its own GPS-scaled sub-maps introduce, whatever weights the edges carry; and a graph of two-view edges cannot reconstitute the many-view coupling that gives bundle adjustment its consistency. These are properties of the formulation, not settings within it, and they are what a future design has to answer for: Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) constraints estimated jointly rather than pairwise, absolute uncertainty-aware GPS priors, and a thin layer of retained structure. How much of the measured gap those limits account for would take the ablations we did not run; we hope the account still saves the next team the same detour. When the approach might be worth revisiting. Several failures trace to the noisy metric anchor, not the formulation. Under an RTK fix, position is accurate to a few centimetres in all of ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) , enough to pin scale across merges and stop inter-sequence constraints conflicting at the meter scale. A lightweight distributed pose graph, with a few sparse retained points supplying the coupling pure SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) / Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) edges cannot, would then deserve a fresh attempt: the negative result is a scoping one, pose-only, GPS-scaled estimation is the wrong tool for consumer -grade capture.
